groups.title: Guide
groups.description: The examples of the design guide, in reading order.

groups.title: The loop language
groups.description: One feature of the loop language each, with comments in the loop script.

groups.title: Loop shapes
groups.description: Graph colouring at n = 5 with each of the five templates; all give the same solutions.

groups.title: Contributed: exists-forall problems
groups.description: One abstraction and one check solver each, in the loop language.

groups.description: More than one check, a solver that computes the refinement, staged searches, or raw Lua.

examples.title: New project
examples.summary: The New project starter: four commented fragments to replace by your own problem.

examples.title: Sum-free sets
examples.summary: Sum-free sets of numbers: the smallest complete CEGAR loop.

examples.title: Sum-free sets (too weak relevant/1)
examples.summary: The same problem with a relevant/1 rule that marks too little: solutions get lost.

examples.title: Guide: one program is not enough
examples.summary: The tempting single program: it finds deletion sets that hit some triangle, not every one.

examples.title: Guide: the guess alone
examples.summary: Only the guess: every set of at most k nodes is accepted.

examples.title: Guide: checking one candidate
examples.summary: One fixed candidate, deleting 4 and 8; the check finds the triangle 1, 2, 3.

examples.title: Guide: blocking one candidate at a time
examples.summary: The first loop: every wrong candidate is blocked on its own (k = 3).

examples.title: Guide: a glue that misses nodes
examples.summary: A glue that misses nodes 8 to 10: the check never sees them deleted, and no solution is left.

examples.title: Guide: cliques of four
examples.summary: Cliques of c = 4 nodes instead of triangles, blocking each wrong candidate.

examples.title: Guide: everything relevant
examples.summary: relevant/1 marks every interface atom: the same run as blocking.

examples.title: Guide: learning from a triangle
examples.summary: A surviving triangle teaches that one of its three nodes must be deleted.

examples.title: Guide: one node of the triangle (unsound)
examples.summary: Too strong: only the busiest node of the triangle is marked, and solutions are lost.

examples.title: Guide: the Paley graph, blocking
examples.summary: The Paley graph (n = 13, k = 6, c = 3), every wrong candidate blocked on its own.

examples.title: Guide: the Paley graph, learning
examples.summary: The Paley graph, one clause per surviving clique (Shape 1).

examples.title: Guide: the Paley graph, enum-mode record
examples.summary: The same with --enum-mode=record on the abstraction: refinements are kept firmly.

examples.title: Guide: thirty counterexamples per candidate
examples.summary: Up to 30 surviving cliques per candidate.

examples.title: Guide: two clauses from one counterexample
examples.summary: The check writes the clauses itself (clause/3): up to two cliques in one counterexample.

examples.title: Guide: sufficient reasons, blocking
examples.summary: Sufficient reasons of at most k = 4 features, blocking each wrong candidate.

examples.title: Guide: sufficient reasons, learning
examples.summary: Sufficient reasons: keep one of the features on which the counterexample differs.

examples.title: Guide: sufficient reasons, smallest counterexample
examples.summary: Sufficient reasons: the check returns a counterexample that differs on as few features as possible.

examples.title: Guide: what the abstraction knows
examples.summary: The triangles among the first m nodes are excluded in the abstraction already.

examples.title: Guide: an abstraction that cuts solutions
examples.summary: Symmetry breaking in the abstraction: "delete node 0" cuts solutions.

examples.title: Guide: triangles through node 0 in advance
examples.summary: The triangles through node 0 are excluded in the abstraction.

examples.title: Guide: Shape 2 on the Paley graph
examples.summary: Shape 2: solve, check, add the clause, solve again.

examples.title: Guide: batches and restarts
examples.summary: Batches: collect counterexamples, restart after 10, add their clauses.

examples.title: Guide: a solution that is not blocked
examples.summary: Shape 2 without blocking the solution: the no-progress guard stops the run.

examples.title: Guide: the clique lesson as a rule
examples.summary: The clique lesson as a rule, grounded once per counterexample (Shape 3).

examples.title: Guide: a refine part without its parameter
examples.summary: A refine part whose heads lack the parameter: the second step changes nothing.

examples.title: Guide: a neighbour of the clique
examples.summary: Exercise: "delete a neighbour of the clique" as a refine part. Is it right?

examples.title: Guide: fair division, blocking
examples.summary: Fair division, blocking each dominated allocation.

examples.title: Guide: fair division, clauses
examples.summary: Fair division with the best clause available: one of the candidate's assignments must change.

examples.title: Guide: 3-colourable graphs, blocking
examples.summary: 3-colourable graphs on n = 5 nodes, blocking each graph without a colouring.

examples.title: Guide: a core from the wrong check
examples.summary: A core taken from a check whose failure means the candidate is good.

examples.title: Guide: minimal sufficient reasons, blocking
examples.summary: Minimal sufficient reasons, blocking every candidate that one of the two checks refutes.

examples.title: Guide: as few deletions as possible
examples.summary: Fewest deletions: candidates smallest first; the first one that survives the check is optimal.

examples.title: Guide: every optimal deletion set
examples.summary: All deletion sets of the smallest size: after the first, a cap forbids larger ones.

examples.title: Guide: plans, the guess alone
examples.summary: Step 1: the guess alone, every sequence of t moves accepted.

examples.title: Guide: plans, blocking
examples.summary: Step 2: the real check, every failing plan blocked on its own.

examples.title: Guide: plans, clauses
examples.summary: Step 3: the best clause marks every move, and is a block in disguise.

examples.title: Guide: plans, rules
examples.summary: Step 4: each failing start cell becomes a copy of the robot inside the abstraction (Shape 3).

examples.title: Loop language: the basics
examples.summary: Declarations, options, variables, loop, if/elif/else, lists, for, count, log, stop, accept.

examples.title: Loop language: several counterexamples
examples.summary: for X in C.models(assume G(M), limit 3): several counterexamples per candidate.

examples.title: Loop language: optimal counterexamples
examples.summary: C.solve(assume G(M), optimal): the smallest refinement, with #minimize in the check.

examples.title: Loop language: two checks
examples.summary: Two check solvers with their own fragments and links; the second runs only if the first finds nothing.

examples.title: Loop language: clauses from ASP
examples.summary: reject M with G.clauses(X): the refinement written as clause/3 atoms in ASP.

examples.title: Loop language: unsat cores
examples.summary: reject M with G.core(C): refine from an unsatisfiable core when the check looks for a witness.

examples.title: Loop language: a refinement solver
examples.summary: A third solver R computes the refinement: R.solve(assume GA(M), GC(X)).

examples.title: Loop language: legacy glue
examples.summary: link ... legacy: glue fragments that list the interface atoms themselves (cegar.py files).

examples.title: Loop language: raw Lua
examples.summary: A loop written directly in Lua against the runtime API (rt.solver, rt.link, A:search, ...).

examples.title: Graph colouring, Shape 1
examples.summary: Shape 1: check inside the search. One solve call of A for the whole run; refinements are added as clauses during the search.

examples.title: Graph colouring, Shape 2
examples.summary: Shape 2: solve, check, refine, solve again. A is solved once per candidate.

examples.title: Graph colouring, Shape 3
examples.summary: Shape 3: ground the #program refine(k) part once per counterexample (rules instead of clauses).

examples.title: Graph colouring, Shape 4
examples.summary: Shape 4: search, collect counterexamples, ground the refine part for 20 at a time.

examples.title: Graph colouring, Reference run
examples.summary: Reference run: block each refuted candidate. Always sound; slow, but its count is the truth.

examples.title: Graph colouring
examples.summary: Graphs with a leaf colouring that no 3-colouring extends (n = 6, all 10,698 solutions).

examples.title: Nash equilibria
examples.summary: Weighted graphs whose colouring game has a Nash equilibrium (four size instances).

examples.title: Voting: justifications
examples.summary: Explaining a voting outcome by axioms: 17 questions as instances, five refinement strategies and two loops as variants, a suite that compares them.

examples.title: Abduction
examples.summary: Propositional abduction: consistent hypothesis sets that entail the observation, with a hidden consistency witness in the abstraction (7 hypotheses, k = 2, 17 solutions).

examples.title: Actual causes
examples.summary: Halpern-Pearl actual causation on the rock-throwing story: witnesses for Suzy's throw being a cause (cause = st, 4 solutions; cause = bt, none).

examples.title: Preferred extensions
examples.summary: Preferred extensions that leave out a query argument (sceptical acceptance), with one refinement clause per added argument (9 arguments, 3 solutions).

examples.title: Semi-stable extensions
examples.summary: Semi-stable extensions of an argumentation framework; the interface is the derived range/1, so clauses speak about ranges (11 arguments, 2 solutions).

examples.title: Agenda safety
examples.summary: Minimally inconsistent subsets of an agenda with three or more formulas, the witnesses that majority voting is unsafe (doctrinal paradox agenda, 6 solutions).

examples.title: Ramsey arrowing
examples.summary: Edge colourings of K_n without a red triangle and without a blue 4-cycle; the check embeds a pattern graph (n = 6, 100 solutions; n = 7, none).

examples.title: Belief update
examples.summary: Updating beliefs by minimal change (possible-models approach): old and new worlds that refute a query, checked against closer worlds (7 atoms, 8 solutions).

examples.title: Boolean games
examples.summary: Pure Nash equilibria of a Boolean game: a counterexample is a player with a profitable deviation (4 players, 8 variables, 6 solutions).

examples.title: List colouring
examples.summary: List assignments from which a graph cannot be properly coloured, refuting choosability (K(3,3), lists of 2 out of 3 colours, 36 solutions).

examples.title: Clique colouring
examples.summary: Two-colourings of the nodes without a one-coloured maximal clique (complement of a cycle, n = 8, 44 solutions).

examples.title: Clique interdiction
examples.summary: Deleting at most k nodes so that no clique of c nodes survives, with up to three counterexample cliques per candidate (Paley graph, n = 13, k = 6, c = 3, 39 solutions).

examples.title: Conformant planning
examples.summary: A sequence of moves that reaches the goal from every start cell; each counterexample start cell is simulated inside the abstraction (Shape 3; t = 8, 3 solutions).

examples.title: Default extensions
examples.summary: Extensions of prerequisite-free normal defaults that entail a query: two kinds of counterexample in one check (Nixon diamond, 7 defaults, 3 solutions).

examples.title: Minimal diagnoses
examples.summary: Minimal diagnoses of a faulty full adder that blame a given gate: minimal models with varying wires (suspect = x2, 2 solutions).

examples.title: Fair and efficient division
examples.summary: Envy-free and Pareto-efficient allocations of indivisible goods; a dominating allocation becomes a rule in the abstraction (Shape 3; 3 agents, 7 goods, 3 solutions).

examples.title: Fewest clues
examples.summary: Puzzles with a unique solution: k clues added to a partly filled 4 x 4 Sudoku; a counterexample is a pair of solutions (k = 2, 64 solutions).

examples.title: Core-stable coalitions
examples.summary: Core-stable partitions of an additively separable hedonic game; relevant/1 uses monotonicity to mark few atoms (6 agents, 2 solutions).

examples.title: Integer expressions
examples.summary: Numbers that one integer expression denotes and another does not (Stockmeyer and Meyer); the candidate is a derived number, its derivation a hidden witness (22 solutions).

examples.title: Kemeny control
examples.summary: Deleting a few voters so that the favourite becomes a Kemeny winner; better rankings are collected and grounded in batches (Shape 4; 7 voters, budget = 2, 3 solutions).

examples.title: Knapsack interdiction
examples.summary: Bilevel knapsack: locked item sets that keep the follower's best profit at or below a bound, with smallest counterexample packings (8 items, 2 solutions).

examples.title: Smallest equivalent DNF
examples.summary: DNF formulas with at most k terms equivalent to a given one: counterexample assignments become clauses over a pool of terms (n = 3, k = 3, 2 solutions).

examples.title: 2QBF by expansion
examples.summary: The 2QBF example with Shape 3: each counterexample y-assignment instantiates the formula in the abstraction (5 solutions).

examples.title: 2QBF, smallest refinement
examples.summary: The 2QBF example with a check that guesses which x-literals to blame and minimises their number (C.solve(..., optimal); 5 solutions).

examples.title: 2QBF
examples.summary: Exists-forall QBF with a DNF matrix: clause refinements from the false x-literals of the open terms (6 + 5 variables, 12 terms, 5 solutions).

examples.title: Smallest unsatisfiable subsets
examples.summary: Unsatisfiable subsets with at most k clauses, by collecting hitting-set constraints from satisfying assignments (12 clauses, k = 4, 2 solutions).

examples.title: Stable models by hand
examples.summary: Stable models of a disjunctive program given as facts: classical models checked against the reduct (11 atoms, 22 rules, 3 solutions).

examples.title: Strategic companies
examples.summary: Strategic sets of companies that contain a given company; minimality is refuted by a smaller set, refined with G.clauses (8 companies, 2 solutions).

examples.title: Strong Nash equilibria
examples.summary: Strong Nash equilibria of a graphical game: a counterexample is a coalition whose members all gain by deviating together (8 players, 1 solution).

examples.title: Subset sum game
examples.summary: Sets of x-numbers that no set of y-numbers completes to the target; the interface is the derived sum, so one clause removes all sets with that sum (7 + 7 numbers, 11 solutions).

examples.title: Sudoku beyond the beginner
examples.summary: A 9 x 9 Sudoku with a unique solution that singles, pairs and locked candidates cannot finish; the beginner is part of the abstraction (k = 26 on a fixed grid; the run stops at the first puzzle).

examples.title: Sudoku with a unique solution
examples.summary: A 9 x 9 Sudoku with k clues and a unique solution, generated from scratch; a counterexample is a pair of solutions (k = 25; the run stops at the first puzzle).

examples.title: Sufficient reasons
examples.summary: Smallest sets of features that force a small neural network's answer on a given input (8 features, k = 3, 2 solutions).

examples.title: Abduction with two checks
examples.summary: Propositional abduction with a witness check (refined by unsat cores) and a counterexample check (7 hypotheses, k = 2, 17 solutions).

examples.title: Conformant planning, growing horizon
examples.summary: Conformant planning without a bound constant: the horizon grows (A.ground, G.extend, externals) until the first plans appear, which are the shortest.

examples.title: Knapsack bounds in Lua
examples.summary: The bilevel knapsack optimisation with numeric bounds: M.value(value/1) and X.value(gain/1) give lower and upper bounds that are logged until they meet (optimum 25, 2 solutions).

examples.title: Knapsack interdiction with fortification
examples.summary: A trilevel knapsack (Sigma-3-complete): three solvers in a chain, with hitting-set clauses learned at both levels (2 solutions of 37 candidates).

examples.title: Knapsack interdiction, optimum
examples.summary: Bilevel knapsack optimisation: an optimal abstraction gives lower bounds, the follower's best replies are grounded as rules, and a second part caps the claims (optimum 25, 2 solutions).

examples.title: Minimal sufficient reasons
examples.summary: Subset-minimal sufficient reasons with two checks: a counterexample for sufficiency, a witness with unsat cores for minimality (8 features, 4 solutions).

examples.title: 2QBF, blame by a third solver
examples.summary: The 2QBF example with a refinement solver that minimises the blamed x-variables for the counterexample at hand (5 solutions).

examples.title: QBF with any number of blocks
examples.summary: A QBF with any number of quantifier blocks: a solver family, a link family and a recursive procedure (def refute) answer each level (depth = 3 here).

examples.title: 3QBF
examples.summary: An exists-forall-exists formula: three solvers in a chain, clauses for the middle solver from witnesses and for the outer one from unsat cores (4 solutions).

examples.title: Reasons by shrinking
examples.summary: Minimal sufficient reasons by shrinking accepted candidates: the assumption list G(M) is walked and edited (a.true, E.flip(a)), and G.above removes the supersets (8 features, 4 solutions).

examples.title: Reasons by size
examples.summary: Minimal sufficient reasons in order of size: an optimal abstraction, and G.above removes the supersets of each solution (8 features, 4 solutions).
